    applicant: An applicant object with attributes

    elif applicant.recommendation_letters == 'medium' :

def factorial(n):
    """
    Calculate the factorial of a number
    :param n: Integer
    :return: Integer
    """
    if n < 0:
        raise ValueError("Input must be a non-negative integer.")
    if not isinstance(n, int):
        raise TypeError("Input must be an integer.")

    result = 1
    for i in range(1, n+1):
        result *= i
    return result

4. Once the loop finishes, it returns the final value of `result`, which is the factorial of the input `n`.

jq is like sed for JSON data - you can use it to slice, filter, map,
and transform structured data, using the same regex, array and object
manipulation tools that you're already familiar with. jq is like sed
or awk, but for JSON data sources.

Any JSON input data for jq is simply passed to the filter as a single
value, this could be either an object, an array, a number, a string, a
Boolean or null.

For more information about jq, see: https://stedolan.github.io/jq/manual/v1.5/

jq also has some additional documentation in the sections below, which explain the above in more detail.

## Installation

See https://stedolan.github.io/jq/download/

## Problem

JSON data is often nested and hard to process by traditional shell
tools, and as JSON is a standard text format, with a syntax very much
unlike many "conf" files, so not directly usable by configuration
management tools.

## Solution

jq is like sed for JSON data, providing a mechanism for lightweight
transformation of the data, combined with a command-line shell tool
that makes handling these files simple.

For example, fetching open issues for the swt repository from GitHub:

```
% curl https://api.github.com/repos/eclipse/swt/issues?state=open \
 | jq .[].title
```

jq could also be used in scripts to merge and extract data from JSON
files, recursively downloading a json data file from a website:

```
#!/bin/bash

fnbasename(){ echo $1|sed 's:.*/::'; }

if [ "$1" == "" ];
then
   echo "Usage: jsonload.sh JSON_URL [MASTER_NAME]"
   exit 0;
fi;

if [ "$2" == "" ];
then
   master_name="master"
else
   master_name=$2
fi;

urlbase=$(echo $1 |sed 's:.*/json$::');

filename=$(fnbasename $1).json
until [ -e $filename ];
do
   echo "Getting " $filename
   wget -q -O $filename $urlbase/json
done;

jq .$master_name $filename;
```

In addition, jq has support for command-line options that let you avoid having to pre-process your data:

```
% curl https://api.github.com/repos/stedolan/jq/issues?state=open \
| jq -r '.[] | {user: .user.login, title: .title}'
```

You can filter arrays, extract values, transform data, nearly anything can be done and you will always get a result in JSON format. :)

jq is like sed for JSON data - you can use it to slice, filter, map,
and transform structured data, using the same regex, array and object
manipulation tools that you're already familiar with.  It can also
output in a variety of JSON-friendly formats like csv, xml and tables.

jq is written in portable C, and it has zero runtime dependencies.  It
implements the same fundamental algorithms as `sed`, `awk`, `grep`,
`join`, etc. (only faster and with more precise semantics).  jq’s API is
simple: it takes a sequence of strings and a JSON object, and returns a
sequence of JSON expressions.

jq uses a new kind of language for querying JSON data - an
incremental, just-in-time compiler to C. This means that jq may need a
different approach to understanding your query than you expect (read
the manual!), and the program is significantly larger and more complex
than similar tools, but on the plus side it’s much faster.

jq has its own [manual](https://stedolan.github.io/jq/manual/v1.5/), which is a good place to start learning about the language or writing queries.
The manual also contains a few examples of what you can do with jq.

jq is maintained by Stephen Dolan ([@stedolan](https://github.com/stedolan)) and hundreds of contributors.  It's free software, and you may redistribute it under the terms of the [MIT licence](https://github.com/stedolan/jq/blob/master/LICENSE.md).

Please [open an issue on GitHub](https://github.com/stedolan/jq/issues).

You’re welcome to [help us fix bugs](https://github.com/stedolan/jq/labels/bug)!

## Building jq

In most cases, you should be able to clone the repository, run `./configure`, `make`, and `sudo make install` to get it working.

If you encounter any problems, make sure you have all the prerequisites installed:

- A relatively recent C compiler (e.g., `gcc`)
- The `oniguruma` and `oniguruma-devel` packages, which you can install with your distribution's package manager

You may also want to install `autotools` (`autoconf`, `automake`, `libtool`), `pkgconfig`, and `meson` (for building `oniguruma`), if they aren't already installed.

Then follow these steps:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/stedolan/jq.git jq
cd jq
autoreconf -i
./configure
make
sudo make install
```

If you're on a platform that the maintainers of `jq` don't regularly use (like Windows or macOS), and you're having trouble building it, you might have more luck asking for help on a platform like StackOverflow.  However, it's always a great idea to make sure you have all the dependencies installed and to post any error messages you're getting.

## Testing jq after building

After building jq, it’s always a good idea to test to see if it works.  To do this, you can run `./test/run-tests`.  This script checks that jq gives the expected output on a large number of example queries.  If it doesn’t, there’s a good chance that you’ve found a bug.  (If it does, please let us know about it!)

## Getting help

If you're having trouble with jq, you can help others by filing an issue to ask a question or report a bug. Make sure to include enough information such that others can reproduce the issue.
